title: Vayikra: offering means nearness
hook: the word for offering comes from the root "to come near"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the alef written small, and Moses' humility. Your line was the small letter. Where did you take up a little less room? Day three hundred eighty-one.

Say the word sacrifice, and loss is close behind. Giving something up. A parent who sacrifices sleep, a soldier who sacrifices everything, a chess player who sacrifices a piece. In everyday speech, a sacrifice is mostly about what you lose. Leviticus is full of what English Bibles call offerings and sacrifices: animals, grain, oil, wine. Read it with only the English, and it can sound like a book about giving things up. The Hebrew word underneath says something else entirely.
screen: `SACRIFICE SOUNDS LIKE LOSS.` → `LEVITICUS IS FULL OF OFFERINGS.` → `THE HEBREW SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: The word is korban, and it comes from the Hebrew root kuf, resh, bet: to be near, to come close. The same root gives karov, near, which in modern Hebrew also means a relative, someone close to you. And the verb in Leviticus for bringing an offering, hikriv, literally means to bring near. So the second verse of the book, in the JPS 1917 translation, "When any man of you bringeth an offering unto the LORD," could be heard as: when one of you brings something near, as a bringing-near, to God. The point of a korban, in the language itself, isn't losing something. It's closing a distance. Some Hasidic teachers noticed the odd word order in the Hebrew of that verse, which can be read as: when a person brings near, of yourselves, an offering. The real offering, they said, is the self. And then history made the question urgent. When the Second Temple was destroyed, the offerings stopped. How do you come near without an altar? The prophet Hosea had already given a phrase for it. In the JPS 1917 translation: "So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips." The Talmud records the teaching that the daily prayers stand in place of the daily offerings, and traditional prayer books still include passages about the offerings in the morning service. In that teaching, what the altar did, closing a distance, is now done with words.
screen: `KORBAN: FROM 'TO COME NEAR'.` · `HIKRIV: TO BRING NEAR.` · `THE REAL OFFERING IS THE SELF.` · `THE OFFERING OF OUR LIPS.` · then, large: `OFFERING MEANS NEARNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: draw near. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've drifted away from. A person you haven't called. A practice you used to keep. A part of yourself you've ignored. If you're someone who prays, maybe God. Don't try to fix the distance all at once. Just picture taking one step closer. A text, a page, a minute, a breath. Notice what that step costs, and what it gives. Then breathe, and stay near it for a while. The bell holds the time.
Korban. An offering, from the root meaning to come near. Not a giving up, but a bringing close.
Your line: offering means nearness. Today, take one small step toward someone or something you've drifted from. Day three hundred eighty-one.

what it means: a korban is a bringing-near, and the word itself is about closing the distance to God.
what a scholar hears: the root q-r-b (near) gives korban and hikriv; Berakhot 26b links the daily prayers to the daily offerings, and Hosea 14:3 speaks of the offering of our lips.
